newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia may soften stand on coffee initiative.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia may soften stand on coffee initiative.

text.p: Indonesia, the world's third-largest coffee producer, could soften its opposition to an African initiative to reduce coffee exports at a gathering of top producers in Brazil, industry sources said on Monday.

They said there was a possibility the Indonesian delegation to the meeting on January 23 could agree on the need to reduce exports in the first half of this year to bolster prices, especially the values of robusta coffee.
But the sources said Indonesia's agreement to participate in the proposed scheme would depend on how much the country, Asia's top coffee producer, would have to reduce exports.

"If the reduction in exports does not place too much of a burden on the shoulders of exporters, Indonesia might be willing to compromise on its previous stand of rejecting any cutbacks," one senior industry source told Reuters.
"The reduction has also to be shared fairly by all producers, not just the robusta producers," said the source, who declined to be identified.

The InterAfrican Coffee Organisation (IACO) has proposed that exports by the 14 members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) be cut by 2.5 million 60-kg bags in the first half of 1997 in a bid to lift poor robusta prices.

The move is supported by Colombia, the world's largest producer after Brazil. Jorge Cardenas, head of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation, said ACPC's existing export programme needed to be revised for the first half of this year.

"We agree that we have to make a revision of the programme and organise the quantity of robusta coffee," he told Reuters after he arrived in Rio De Janeiro for a three-day international coffee seminar ahead of the ACPC meeting.
Under a plan agreed to by ACPC members in May last year, members' exports in the January to June period should not exceed 26.28 million bags.
The industry sources said Indonesia was concerned over declining robusta prices, and would be willing to negotiate the proposed cutbacks at the Brazil meeting.
"Indonesia will be willing to reduce exports by about 150,000 bags in the first half of this year," one source said. "Anything more could make it difficult for exporters."
Another source said higher reductions would not be practical as the country's coffee harvest would begin to gather steam from April, when African harvests would be mostly over.
"Vietnam's harvest will be over by February, and it will seem like only Indonesia's exports would be affected," he said. "Vietnam's production is already two-thirds of Indonesia's."
Vietnam, Indonesia's coffee trade rival in Asia, is not an ACPC member and is not bound to participate in the export cuts.
"If we restrain our supplies, there are free riders in the region who will take our market," Paian Nainggolan, Indonesia's representative to the ACPC, said last month.

Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters (AICE) -- who will attend the ACPC meeting in Brazil -- said last Thursday that Indonesia was "open to discussion" on the African initiative.
He said Indonesia was concerned by the differences in prices between arabica and robusta coffee, and would raise the issue at the ACPC meeting in Brazil.
